query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In homogeneous, single‐phase high-entropy alloys, service-relevant thermal and mechanical loading activates diffusion-driven modifications at grain boundaries that produce localized chemical ordering or segregation. This in turn reduces grain-boundary cohesion and facilitates intergranular crack initiation, thereby causing a decrease in toughness that is distinct from the conventional precipitation/segregation mechanisms observed in traditional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy with a uniform, compositionally complex matrix and clean grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled thermal cycling combined with mechanical loading (e.g., cyclic or slow tensile loading) designed to promote grain-boundary chemical ordering or segregation.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under service-relevant temperatures and loading rates that activate diffusion while preserving the overall single-phase structure.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries that develop localized chemical heterogeneities (in the form of either short-range ordering or segregation of minor alloying elements) leading to regions of increased stiffness and reduced ductility.
generation.mechanism: Under applied thermal and mechanical stresses, atomic diffusion is enhanced at grain boundaries, promoting local chemical reordering. This localized modification reduces the cohesive strength of the grain boundaries, thereby facilitating intergranular crack initiation and brittle failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline state, treated samples exhibiting enhanced grain-boundary ordering/segregation will show a measurable reduction in fracture toughness and a shift toward intergranular crack propagation.
generation.baseline: The as-processed, homogeneous single-phase high-entropy alloy with minimal grain-boundary chemical heterogeneity and high fracture toughness.
generation.boundary: The observed mechanism is expected under service-relevant temperatures and mechanical loading conditions; it may not manifest under static, low-temperature, or high-strain-rate conditions where diffusion kinetics are significantly altered.
generation.uncertainty: The precise diffusion kinetics and the degree of local ordering required to trigger measurable embrittlement remain to be quantitatively determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to a controlled program of thermal cycling combined with mechanical loading designed to induce grain-boundary chemical ordering/segregation, while maintaining a control set under isothermal low-stress conditions that suppress such modifications. Post-treatment, perform comparative microstructural and mechanical analyses.
measurements: Grain-boundary composition and degree of chemical ordering/segregation (using atom probe tomography or TEM-EDS)
Fracture toughness measurements (e.g., via standard fracture mechanics tests)
Fractographic analysis to determine whether crack initiation is predominantly intergranular
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally and mechanically treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in fracture toughness or show no evidence of enhanced grain-boundary chemical heterogeneity (relative to control samples), then the hypothesis—that stress-activated grain-boundary ordering/segregation drives brittle behavior in high-entropy alloys—will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In compositionally complex single-phase high-entropy alloys (HEAs), service-related mechanical loading activates solute diffusion that leads to localized segregation along intra-granular defects (e.g., dislocation networks and sub-grain boundaries), which in turn forms nanoscale embrittling regions and triggers brittle behavior. This mechanism is distinct from the conventional alloy failure mode, where toughness loss is predominantly linked to grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitation.
drafts.material_initial_state: A homogenous, single-phase high-entropy alloy with complex composition and an initially uniform solute distribution that suppresses rapid grain coarsening and conventional intermetallic precipitation.
drafts.intervention: Subject the HEA to cyclic or slow tensile loading at service-relevant temperatures (i.e., conditions that enhance diffusion kinetics without causing grain coarsening) to trigger stress-activated solute diffusion.
drafts.conditions: Mechanical loading (cyclic or slow tensile strain) at moderate to high service temperatures that promote diffusion but avoid conventional grain-boundary coarsening; concurrently, a controlled comparison is performed on a conventional alloy under similar conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: Localized solute enrichment along intra-granular defects such as dislocation networks and sub-grain boundaries acting as precursors to nanoscale embrittling regions.
drafts.mechanism: Under mechanical loading, enhanced diffusion permits selective solute segregation at stress concentrators within the grain interior, forming localized phases that lower the toughness and facilitate brittle fracture, rather than relying on pre-existing or forming grain-boundary precipitates.
drafts.predicted_outcome: In the HEA, one should observe the emergence of nanoscale regions with altered composition specifically along dislocation networks prior to, or concomitant with, the onset of brittle fracture. This is expected to occur at lower strains compared with the as-processed baseline, and the mechanism of embrittlement will be distinct from conventional alloys, where grain-boundary precipitation dominates.
drafts.baseline: The initial virgin, homogeneous single-phase state with uniform solute distribution and no identifiable embrittling precipitates.
drafts.boundary: Service-like loading conditions (such as cyclic or low strain rate tensile tests) at elevated temperatures that activate atomic diffusion but avoid inducing significant grain growth or traditional intermetallic precipitation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare single-phase HEA samples and, as a control, conventional alloy samples. Subject both to controlled cyclic or slow tensile loading at service-relevant temperatures. Use in-situ high-resolution microscopy techniques (such as transmission electron microscopy combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy and atom probe tomography) to monitor local compositional changes at intra-granular defects during loading.
measurements: Quantitative mapping of solute distribution along dislocation networks and sub-grain boundaries via atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM-EDS.
Mechanical testing (tensile or cyclic loading) to record the onset strain for brittle behavior in both HEA and conventional alloy samples.
In-situ detection of localized embrittling regions preceding crack initiation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no measurable localized solute enrichment at intra-granular defects is observed in the HEA under the prescribed loading conditions, or if the onset of brittle behavior correlates solely with grain-boundary phenomena (as seen in the conventional alloy), then the hypothesis—that stress-activated intra-granular solute segregation is responsible for brittleness—will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs), exposure to service-relevant thermal cycling and mechanical loading induces stress‐driven segregation of minor alloying elements to grain boundaries. This segregation creates localized compositional heterogeneities that weaken grain boundary cohesion, leading to brittle fracture—a mechanism distinct from the conventional intermetallic precipitation observed in traditional alloys.
drafts.material_initial_state: An initially homogeneous, single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with uniformly distributed elements and clean grain boundaries.
drafts.intervention: Subject HEA specimens to controlled thermal cycling and mechanical loading designed to promote grain boundary segregation versus a baseline processing route that minimizes such segregation.
drafts.conditions: Experiments should mimic service conditions, including cyclic thermal treatments and strain rates representative of operational stresses, while also ensuring that comparisons with conventional processing are made under identical loading and environmental conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: Grain boundary regions that develop local compositional heterogeneities due to the segregation of minor alloying elements.
drafts.mechanism: Under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading, the diffusion kinetics in the HEA favor the migration of certain alloying elements to grain boundaries. This localized enrichment disrupts the cohesive strength of the boundaries, promoting embrittlement without the formation of classic, detectable intermetallic phases. This mechanism contrasts with conventional alloys where embrittlement is primarily due to pronounced grain-boundary precipitation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: HEAs undergoing the segregation-promoting treatment will show a reduction in fracture toughness, with crack initiation localized at grain boundaries exhibiting compositional heterogeneity. In contrast, the baseline samples (with minimized segregation) should maintain higher toughness. Conventional alloy behavior would typically correlate toughness loss with visible intermetallic precipitates rather than subtle segregation.
drafts.baseline: HEA samples processed under isothermal or low-stress conditions that do not favor significant grain boundary segregation, maintaining uniform composition at grain boundaries and higher toughness.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies under service-relevant thermal and mechanical loading conditions. Its applicability may be limited outside these conditions, such as in very low or extremely high temperature regimes or under non-cyclic loading where diffusion kinetics differ significantly.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA specimens. One set undergoes a controlled program of thermal cycling combined with mechanical loading to promote grain boundary segregation, while the control set is maintained under conditions designed to suppress such segregation (e.g., isothermal annealing with minimal stress). Post-treatment, perform microstructural analysis focusing on grain boundary chemistry using techniques like atom probe tomography or TEM-EDS, and measure fracture toughness via standardized fracture mechanics tests.
measurements: Grain boundary composition and distribution (using atom probe tomography or TEM-EDS)
Fractography to identify crack initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in fracture toughness or if no measurable grain boundary segregation is detected (relative to baseline samples), then the hypothesis that stress-induced grain boundary segregation leads to brittle behavior in HEAs is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In single‐phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys, brittle behavior can emerge due to the formation of localized short‐range order at grain boundaries, which creates regions of increased local stiffness and reduced ability to accommodate strain. This effect promotes intergranular crack initiation under mechanical loading, distinguishing it from the conventional segregation/precipitation mechanisms seen in typical alloys.
drafts.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single‐phase high-entropy alloy with a uniform, complex composition and minimal pre-existing short‐range order at grain boundaries.
drafts.intervention: Apply controlled heat-treatment regimes designed to either enhance or suppress the development of short‐range order at grain boundaries without inducing any secondary phases.
drafts.conditions: Mechanical testing under service-relevant conditions (e.g., tensile loading at typical operating temperatures and strain rates) while maintaining the overall alloy composition.
drafts.structural_mediator: Localized short‐range order motifs at grain boundaries that result in regions with higher stiffness and reduced plasticity.
drafts.mechanism: Heat treatments induce local atomic rearrangements that lead to short-range ordering near grain boundaries. This local ordering increases the elastic modulus and decreases ductility at specific regions, thereby acting as preferential sites for intergranular crack propagation when the alloy is subjected to mechanical stress.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Samples with enhanced short-range order at the grain boundaries will show a measurable decrease in toughness (i.e., earlier onset of brittle fracture) compared to control samples with suppressed ordering, despite both sets being single‐phase and compositionally similar.
drafts.baseline: A high-entropy alloy with minimal grain-boundary short-range order exhibiting a favorable strength–ductility combination and ductile failure mode.
drafts.boundary: The predicted behavior is expected under service-relevant mechanical loading conditions and within temperature regimes typical of engineering applications. The effect may differ if extreme temperatures or strain rates are applied.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of high-entropy alloy samples with identical overall composition. One group undergoes a heat-treatment that promotes the development of short-range order at the grain boundaries; the other group is treated to suppress such ordering. Both sets are then subjected to identical tensile tests under controlled conditions.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of grain-boundary short-range order (e.g., via atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM)
Fractographic analysis to identify the mode of crack propagation (intergranular versus transgranular)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with induced grain-boundary short-range order do not exhibit lower toughness or show no significant increase in intergranular fracture relative to the control samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In single‐phase high-entropy alloys, service-relevant thermal and mechanical loading can activate stress-assisted local chemical ordering at grain boundaries, which in turn promotes the formation of nanoscale brittle intermetallic precursors that degrade toughness.
drafts.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex high-entropy alloy in a uniform single-phase state with no detectable segregation or secondary phases.
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloy to elevated temperatures combined with cyclic mechanical loading representative of demanding service conditions.
drafts.conditions: High-temperature exposure and mechanical fatigue cycling (conditions that are more stringent than those typically encountered by conventional alloys, where grain-boundary segregation typically governs brittleness).
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of localized, nanoscale clusters or chemically ordered domains at grain boundaries and triple junctions.
drafts.mechanism: Under high-temperature mechanical stressing, diffusion becomes activated even in compositionally complex alloys, leading to local short-range ordering at grain boundaries. This local ordering reduces the entropy stabilization locally and promotes the nucleation of brittle intermetallic precursors, thereby reducing toughness.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline state, the alloy subjected to these service conditions would show a measurable reduction in fracture toughness correlated with the appearance of nanoscale ordered clusters along grain boundaries, a behavior distinct from conventional alloys that fail primarily due to macroscopic grain-boundary segregation.
drafts.baseline: The initial uniformly mixed single-phase high-entropy alloy with high toughness and resistance to conventional grain-boundary embrittlement.
drafts.boundary: The observed mechanism is expected under high-temperature cyclic loading and may not be significant under static, low-stress, or room-temperature conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one with the standard composition and another modified to include elements that inhibit diffusion-driven ordering (e.g., by increasing the activation energy for diffusion). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature mechanical cycling. Use atom probe tomography (APT) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to characterize grain-boundary chemistry and morphology, and perform fracture toughness measurements.
measurements: Microstructural identification of nanoscale clusters via TEM
Fracture toughness and crack propagation behavior under load
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If (a) the standard alloy does not exhibit significant local chemical ordering at grain boundaries after treatment, or (b) the toughness degradation does not correlate with the presence or extent of such ordering (or if both standard and modified alloys show similar behavior), then the hypothesis that stress-activated local ordering drives brittle behavior is falsified.
